text: Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service — and if that name doesn't ring a bell yet, its old name probably will. Microsoft renamed Azure Active Directory to Microsoft Entra ID in 2023, as part of a broader rebrand of its identity products. Same underlying directory, new name, and it's the service standing behind every single sign-in to the Azure portal, Microsoft 365, and Azure itself — everything you've touched so far in this course.

Here's the distinction that actually matters, and it isn't just a marketing name change. Entra ID is cloud-native, not a hosted copy of on-prem Active Directory. Traditional AD runs on domain controllers — servers you install, patch, and keep running yourself — and clients authenticate using Kerberos while querying the directory over LDAP. Entra ID has none of that. It's managed entirely through REST calls to the Microsoft Graph API over HTTPS, the same way a modern SaaS product exposes its data.

A tenant is a single dedicated Entra ID directory belonging to one organization, identified by a unique ID and a *.onmicrosoft.com domain. Every Azure subscription is linked to exactly one tenant, which is what makes the tenant the real trust boundary in Azure — a subscription trusts its tenant to vouch for who's signing in, and nothing outside it gets access without an explicit relationship being configured.

So when the Azure portal lists your users, that list comes from a Graph API call happening behind the scenes. When a PowerShell script creates a new account, it's making the exact same kind of call. This API-first design is exactly why Entra ID scales the way it does and is reachable from anywhere with an internet connection — it was built for the cloud from day one, not retrofitted from a protocol designed for a private office network.

When you sign into portal.azure.com, there's no domain controller on a LAN checking a Kerberos ticket. Your browser is redirected to Entra ID's sign-in endpoint, your credentials — and an MFA challenge, if required — are verified over HTTPS, and a token comes back proving who you are. That token drives the rest of your session. Next up: the users, groups, and licenses that actually live inside that tenant.
